entry.title: Pung v. Isabella County
entry.content: PRELIMINARY PRINT Volume 609 U. S. Part 1 Pages 30–58 OFFICIAL REPORTS OF THE SUPREME COURT June 23, 2026 REBECCA A. WOMELDORF reporter of decisions Page Proof Pending Publication NOTICE: This preliminary print is subject to formal revision before the bound volume is published. Users are requested to notify the Reporter of Decisions, Supreme Court of the United States, Washington, D. C. 20543, pio@supremecourt.gov, of any typographical or other formal errors. 30 OCTOBER TERM, 2025 Syllabus PUNG, PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVE OF THE ESTATE OF PUNG v. ISABELLA COUNTY, MICHIGAN certiorari to the united states court of appeals for the sixth circuit No. 25–95. Argued February 25, 2026—Decided June 23, 2026 The Pung family owed $2,241.93 in real-property taxes, so local tax author- ities in Isabella County, Michigan, initiated foreclosure proceedings and sold the Pung home—which was assessed at $194,400 for tax purposes— for $76,008 at public auction. Michael Pung sued in Federal court, and the District Court granted Pung partial summary judgment on his Fifth Amendment claim. The court held that Pung should receive only the surplus proceeds from the tax sale—i. e., the difference between the sale price and the tax debt—not the property's fair market value. The District Court also rejected Pung's claim under the Eighth Amendment Excessive Fines Clause. The Sixth Circuit affrmed. Held: 1. The proper baseline for measuring “just compensation” following a tax sale is the auction sale price, not the property's hypothetical fair market value, at least when the sale is fairly conducted in light of the country's history of tax sales. Pp. 35–43. (a) For hundreds of years, English and American law have allowed the seizure and sale of property as a tax-collection method, provided that the government return any surplus proceeds to the debtor. entry.title: Landor v. Louisiana Dept of Corrections and Public Safety
entry.content: PRELIMINARY PRINT Volume 609 U. S. Part 1 Pages 59–107 OFFICIAL REPORTS OF THE SUPREME COURT June 23, 2026 REBECCA A. WOMELDORF reporter of decisions Page Proof Pending Publication NOTICE: This preliminary print is subject to formal revision before the bound volume is published. Users are requested to notify the Reporter of Decisions, Supreme Court of the United States, Washington, D. C. 20543, pio@supremecourt.gov, of any typographical or other formal errors. Page Proof Pending Publication OCTOBER TERM, 2025 59 Syllabus LANDOR v. LOUISIANA DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS AND PUBLIC SAFETY et al. certiorari to the united states court of appeals for the fth circuit No. 23–1197. Argued November 10, 2025—Decided June 23, 2026 The Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act of 2000 (RLUIPA) was enacted pursuant to Congress's Spending Clause author- ity and imposes various conditions on federal funds distributed to state prison systems like the Louisiana Department of Corrections (LDOC). One condition requires state prison systems to agree to answer federal suits by private plaintiffs alleging certain substantial burdens on their re- ligious exercises. See 42 U. S. C. §§ 2000cc–1(a), (b)(1). Relying on that provision, inmate Damon Landor brought this RLUIPA lawsuit against LDOC as well as some of the prison system's individual offcers in their personal capacities, seeking damages from them. Mr. Landor is a Rastafarian whose religious convictions require him to leave his hair uncut. He claims that LDOC offcers—despite being aware of his reli- gious beliefs—forcibly shaved his head. The offcers moved to dismiss, arguing that while their employer LDOC may have agreed to answer cer- tain private suits under RLUIPA, they were not parties to any such agreement, and therefore Mr. Landor had no federal cause of action against them. The district court dismissed Mr. Landor's RLUIPA claims against both the offcers and LDOC. On appeal, Mr. Landor

entry.content: PRELIMINARY PRINT Volume 609 U. S. Part 1 Pages 108–140 OFFICIAL REPORTS OF THE SUPREME COURT June 23, 2026 REBECCA A. Page Proof Pending Publication 108 OCTOBER TERM, 2025 Syllabus EXXON MOBIL CORP. v. CORPORACIÓN CIMEX, S. A. (CUBA), et al. certiorari to the united states court of appeals for the district of columbia circuit No. 24–699. Argued February 23, 2026—Decided June 23, 2026 In 1960, after Fidel Castro seized power in Cuba, the Cuban Government confscated many foreign-owned assets, including Exxon's oil refnery, terminals, packaging plants, and more than a hundred service stations. Since then, two Cuban government-owned companies—Unión Cuba- Petróleo (CUPET) and Corporación CIMEX, S. A. (Cuba) (CIMEX)— have operated and profted from Exxon's expropriated assets. Exxon had no good way to sue the Cuban government entities and seek com- pensation for its confscated property until Congress passed and Presi- dent Clinton signed the Helms-Burton Act in 1996. As relevant here, the Act created a private right of action for U. S. nationals whose prop- erty was confscated by the Cuban Government against “any person that . . . traffcs in” the confscated property, 22 U. S. C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), with “person” defned to include “any agency or instrumentality of a foreign state,” § 6023(11). Exxon sued CUPET, CIMEX, and later CIMEX's Panamanian alter ego under the Helms-Burton Act in the U. S. District Court for the District of Columbia, seeking more than $1 billion in dam- ages. entry.content: PRELIMINARY PRINT Volume 609 U. S. Part 1 Pages 185–257 OFFICIAL REPORTS OF THE SUPREME COURT June 25, 2026 REBECCA A. Page Proof Pending Publication OCTOBER TERM, 2025 185 Syllabus WOLFORD et al. v. LOPEZ, ATTORNEY GENERAL OF HAWAII certiorari to the united states court of appeals for the ninth circuit No. 24–1046. Argued January 20, 2026—Decided June 25, 2026 For years, the State of Hawaii made it almost impossible to obtain a li- cense to carry a frearm. Four years ago, however, this Court held in New York State Rife & Pistol Assn., Inc. v. Bruen, 597 U. S. 1, that the Second and Fourteenth Amendments protect the right to carry hand- guns outside the home for self-defense. Hawaii responded by replacing its old law on carry permits with new laws that achieved a similar result. At issue in this case is a Hawaii law that prohibits frearms on private property open to the public without the express and affrmative consent of the property owner. Hawaii's new rule imposes severe restrictions on the daily activities of residents who have satisfed the State's rigor- ous requirements for the issuance of a carry permit. When these per- mit holders leave home, not only must they take care to avoid all the territory where the possession of a gun is prohibited outright, but they may also be barred from entering many places that people routinely visit in the course of their daily routines, such as gas stations, restau- rants, and stores. entry.title: National PA Week - October 6 through 12
entry.content:
WHEREAS, quality, cost-effective, and patient-centered healthcare is essential to the well-being and quality of life of all people in Maine; and


WHEREAS, physician associates/assistants (PAs) are nationally certified and state-licensed medical professionals who diagnose illnesses, develop and manage treatment plans, prescribe medications, and often serve as a patient's principal healthcare provider; and


WHEREAS, PAs are trusted providers and vital members of the healthcare team, enhancing access to high-quality care in primary care settings, hospitals, rural communities, and underserved areas; and
 

WHEREAS, PAs deliver compassionate, expert care, often serving as the first point of contact for patients and empowering individuals and families to be active participants in their own health; and
 

WHEREAS, PAs provide critical care across a broad range of medical specialties, including addressing the growing demand for behavioral and mental health services by offering compassionate, evidence-based care to individuals and families in need; and
 

WHEREAS, PAs are committed to addressing health disparities, expanding access, and providing team-based, person-centered care across every medical specialty and setting; and
 

WHEREAS, PAs have earned the respect of patients and colleagues alike for their clinical excellence, adaptability, and deep dedication to the communities they serve; and
 

WHEREAS, Maine has been a leader in progressing PA practice and ensuring access to PA services by enacting legislation in recent years to join the PA compact, change the title of the profession to accurately reflect the scope of the profession, and allow PAs to practice at the top of their education and training;


NOW, THEREFORE, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim October 6-12, 2026 as 

National PA Week

in Maine, and I encourage all residents to recognize and celebrate the important role that PAs play in improving health, advancing equity, and delivering high-quality care across the healthcare system.

In testimony whereof, I have caused

the Great Seal of the State to be

hereunto affixed GIVEN under my

hand at Augusta this twenty ninth day of

September Two Thousand Twenty-Six

(CUBA), et al. certiorari to the united states court of appeals for the district of columbia circuit No. 24–699. Argued February 23, 2026—Decided June 23, 2026 In 1960, after Fidel Castro seized power in Cuba, the Cuban Government confscated many foreign-owned assets, including Exxon's oil refnery, terminals, packaging plants, and more than a hundred service stations. Since then, two Cuban government-owned companies—Unión Cuba- Petróleo (CUPET) and Corporación CIMEX, S. A. (Cuba) (CIMEX)— have operated and profted from Exxon's expropriated assets. Exxon had no good way to sue the Cuban government entities and seek com- pensation for its confscated property until Congress passed and Presi- dent Clinton signed the Helms-Burton Act in 1996. As relevant here, the Act created a private right of action for U. S. nationals whose prop- erty was confscated by the Cuban Government against “any person that . . . traffcs in” the confscated property, 22 U. S. C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), with “person” defned to include “any agency or instrumentality of a foreign state,” § 6023(11). Exxon sued CUPET, CIMEX, and later CIMEX's Panamanian alter ego under the Helms-Burton Act in the U. S. District Court for the District of Columbia, seeking more than $1 billion in dam- ages.
